Unit: Unit 1 · Senior Inquiry and Political Analysis
Title: Senior Inquiry and the Social Sciences
Essential Question: How can a senior distinguish a defensible social-science conclusion from an opinion, slogan, or unsupported prediction?
Focus: Comparative inquiry using political science, history, economics, geography, law, sociology, and ethical reasoning.
Performance: Senior Inquiry Diagnostic and Research Notebook Charter
Source Laboratory: United Nations Human Development data, constitutions, election records, and public-opinion evidence

Unit: Unit 1 · Senior Inquiry and Political Analysis
Title: Evidence, Methodology, and Academic Integrity
Essential Question: What procedures make research credible, ethical, reproducible, and honest?
Focus: Source authority, triangulation, research ethics, citation, plagiarism prevention, disclosure of AI assistance, and data integrity.
Performance: Verified Source Dossier and Academic Integrity Agreement
Source Laboratory: Stanford Civic Online Reasoning, research ethics protocols, and citation standards

Unit: Unit 2 · Power, Regimes, and Political Ideas
Title: Power, Authority, Legitimacy, and Sovereignty
Essential Question: Why do people obey political institutions, and when does power become legitimate authority?
Focus: Coercive, economic, institutional, structural, and persuasive power; internal and external sovereignty.
Performance: Power and Legitimacy Concept Application Essay
Source Laboratory: Max Weber’s types of authority, constitutional preambles, and recognition of states

Unit: Unit 2 · Power, Regimes, and Political Ideas
Title: Political Ideologies and Models of Justice
Essential Question: How do political ideologies define freedom, equality, authority, property, obligation, and justice?
Focus: Liberalism, conservatism, socialism, nationalism, feminism, environmentalism, religious political thought, and plural models of justice.
Source Laboratory: Selections from Locke, Burke, Mill, Marx, Rawls, Indigenous political thought, and contemporary voices

Unit: Unit 2 · Power, Regimes, and Political Ideas
Title: Regimes, Democracy, and Authoritarianism
Essential Question: Which institutional evidence distinguishes democracy, hybrid regimes, and authoritarian rule?
Focus: Electoral democracy, liberal democracy, one-party systems, military rule, personalist rule, competitive authoritarianism, and democratic erosion.
Source Laboratory: Freedom House methodology, V-Dem indicators, constitutional rules, and election-observer reports

Unit: Unit 2 · Power, Regimes, and Political Ideas
Title: Constitutions, Federalism, and Unitary States
Essential Question: How do constitutional design and territorial organization distribute power and manage diversity?
Focus: Written and unwritten constitutions, federalism, devolution, unitary government, amendment, emergency power, and constitutional endurance.
Source Laboratory: United States, United Kingdom, India, Nigeria, Mexico, and South Africa constitutional structures

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Executives, Legislatures, and Bureaucracies
Essential Question: How do presidential, parliamentary, and hybrid systems organize leadership, representation, and administration?
Focus: Presidential and parliamentary executives, cabinets, legislatures, confidence votes, coalition government, bureaucratic capacity, and oversight.
Performance: Institutional Power Map and Accountability Memo
Source Laboratory: Cabinet formation, legislative oversight records, and comparative executive powers

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Courts, Rule of Law, and Accountability
Essential Question: When can courts constrain political power, and what makes judicial independence credible?
Focus: Judicial review, constitutional courts, common and civil law traditions, appointment, tenure, access to justice, corruption control, and transitional justice.
Source Laboratory: Constitutional court decisions from multiple legal traditions and anti-corruption institutions

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Parties and Electoral Systems
Essential Question: How do electoral rules shape parties, representation, coalition building, and accountability?
Focus: Plurality, majority, proportional, mixed systems, district magnitude, thresholds, party systems, candidate selection, and malapportionment.
Source Laboratory: Election laws and results from the UK, Mexico, Nigeria, India, Germany, and South Africa

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Voting, Representation, and Public Opinion
Essential Question: How can citizens and analysts determine whether political participation is meaningful, equal, informed, and representative?
Focus: Turnout, franchise, registration, compulsory voting, public-opinion sampling, weighting, margins of error, representation, and political efficacy.
Source Laboratory: Election administration data, public-opinion methodology reports, and representation statistics
Capstone Checkpoint: Source Map and Annotated Bibliography I
Major Assessment: Electoral System and Public Opinion Analysis

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Civil Society, Interest Groups, and Social Movements
Essential Question: How do people organize outside government to influence law, culture, institutions, and public priorities?
Focus: Civil society, advocacy, unions, professional associations, religious organizations, social movements, protest, repression, resource mobilization, and political opportunity.
Source Laboratory: Civil-rights, labor, anti-corruption, environmental, democratic, and nationalist movement records

Unit: Unit 3 · Comparative Institutions and Participation
Title: Media, Propaganda, and Political Communication
Essential Question: How can citizens evaluate political information when governments, parties, platforms, journalists, and networks compete to shape attention?
Focus: Press systems, censorship, ownership, agenda setting, framing, propaganda, disinformation, algorithms, verification, and information resilience.
Source Laboratory: The Verifier, press-freedom reports, platform transparency records, and selected propaganda artifacts

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: United Kingdom and Mexico
Essential Question: How do two electoral democracies with different constitutional histories distribute power, representation, and accountability?
Focus: UK parliamentary sovereignty, devolution, constitutional conventions, first-past-the-post; Mexico’s federal presidency, multiparty competition, electoral reform, and state capacity.
Source Laboratory: UK Parliament, Electoral Commission, Mexico’s Constitution, INE records, and comparative data

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: Nigeria and India
Essential Question: How do large, diverse federal democracies manage identity, development, representation, and uneven state capacity?
Focus: Federalism, ethnicity, religion, language, party competition, judicial institutions, corruption, development, and regional inequality.
Source Laboratory: Constitutions, election data, census evidence, development indicators, and court decisions

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: China and Russia
Essential Question: How do major authoritarian states maintain control while adapting institutions, markets, nationalism, and technology?
Focus: One-party rule, party-state institutions, personalism, federal form, managed elections, censorship, state capitalism, nationalism, and coercive capacity.
Source Laboratory: Constitutions, party documents, election records, economic data, and information-control studies

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: Iran, Brazil, and South Africa
Essential Question: How do constitutional design, identity, inequality, social movements, and political conflict shape different paths of change?
Focus: Iran’s theocratic-republican institutions; Brazil’s presidential federalism and coalition politics; South Africa’s constitutional democracy and post-apartheid transformation.
Source Laboratory: Constitutions, court decisions, election results, protest records, and inequality indicators

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: Comparative Political Systems Synthesis
Essential Question: Which concepts best explain similarities and differences across political systems without erasing history and context?
Focus: Most-similar and most-different systems, case selection, typologies, causal inference, institutional comparison, and evidence qualification.
Source Laboratory: Country portfolios from Weeks 13–16 and cross-national governance datasets

Unit: Unit 4 · Comparative Country Laboratories
Title: Semester Examination and Capstone Proposal Defense
Essential Question: Can the student integrate comparative concepts, institutional evidence, country knowledge, and a defensible research plan?
Focus: Cumulative comparative politics examination, proposal, preliminary bibliography, method, ethics, feasibility, and oral defense.
Performance: Semester Examination and Capstone Proposal Defense
Source Laboratory: Semester evidence portfolio and capstone checkpoint record

Unit: Unit 5 · International Relations and Global Governance
Title: International Relations Theories
Essential Question: How do competing theories explain state behavior, institutions, identity, conflict, and cooperation?
Focus: Realism, liberal institutionalism, constructivism, Marxist and dependency approaches, feminist IR, postcolonial perspectives, and levels of analysis.
Source Laboratory: Selected diplomatic crises and international cooperation cases

Unit: Unit 5 · International Relations and Global Governance
Title: Foreign Policy and National Interest
Essential Question: How should governments define national interest when security, prosperity, values, law, and domestic politics conflict?
Focus: Foreign-policy decision making, executive and legislative roles, bureaucratic politics, public opinion, strategic culture, interests, values, and unintended consequences.
Source Laboratory: Declassified decision records, executive statements, legislative debates, and outcome data

Unit: Unit 5 · International Relations and Global Governance
Title: Diplomacy, Negotiation, and Statecraft
Essential Question: How can actors negotiate durable agreements when interests, power, information, and trust differ?
Focus: Diplomacy, bargaining, mediation, signaling, leverage, reservation points, issue linkage, verification, and implementation.
Source Laboratory: Treaty negotiations, peace processes, trade bargaining, and diplomatic communications

Unit: Unit 5 · International Relations and Global Governance
Title: International Organizations and Global Governance
Essential Question: When can international organizations solve collective problems, and when do power, design, or sovereignty limit them?
Focus: United Nations, Security Council, General Assembly, regional organizations, World Trade Organization, World Bank, IMF, World Health Organization, nonstate actors, and institutional legitimacy.
Source Laboratory: UN Charter, institutional voting rules, budgets, reports, and evaluations

Unit: Unit 6 · International Law, Rights, and Human Mobility
Title: International Law, Treaties, and Courts
Essential Question: How does international law create obligations without a single global sovereign?
Focus: Treaties, custom, general principles, jurisdiction, state responsibility, international courts, international criminal law, humanitarian law, and enforcement.
Source Laboratory: UN Charter, Vienna Convention principles, ICJ and ICC materials, and Geneva law

Unit: Unit 6 · International Law, Rights, and Human Mobility
Title: Human Rights and Humanitarian Principles
Essential Question: How should universal rights be interpreted, protected, and enforced across diverse societies and unequal power?
Focus: Universal Declaration, civil and political rights, economic and social rights, group rights, derogation, proportionality, monitoring, advocacy, and cultural debate.
Source Laboratory: Universal Declaration, core treaties, court decisions, and documented monitoring reports

Unit: Unit 6 · International Law, Rights, and Human Mobility
Title: Migration, Refugees, Citizenship, and Statelessness
Essential Question: How should states balance borders, sovereignty, labor needs, family unity, humanitarian protection, and equal dignity?
Focus: Voluntary and forced migration, refugee law, asylum, internally displaced persons, citizenship, statelessness, diaspora, remittances, integration, detention, and burden sharing.
Source Laboratory: Refugee Convention materials, UNHCR data, migration statistics, and national policies

Unit: Unit 7 · Development, Political Economy, and Global Challenges
Title: Development, Poverty, and Global Inequality
Essential Question: How should development be measured, explained, financed, and evaluated?
Focus: GDP, human development, poverty measures, capability, institutions, colonial legacies, gender, health, education, infrastructure, aid, and sustainable development.
Source Laboratory: UNDP, World Bank, national statistics, Sustainable Development Goals, and program evaluations
Capstone Checkpoint: Annotated Bibliography II and Preliminary Analysis

Unit: Unit 7 · Development, Political Economy, and Global Challenges
Title: Global Political Economy, Trade, and Debt
Essential Question: Who gains, who loses, and who decides in systems of global trade, finance, investment, taxation, and debt?
Focus: Comparative advantage, trade agreements, supply chains, foreign investment, sanctions, sovereign debt, financial crises, tax competition, labor, and distribution.
Source Laboratory: WTO records, trade data, sovereign-debt cases, supply-chain maps, and labor evidence

Unit: Unit 7 · Development, Political Economy, and Global Challenges
Title: Climate, Resources, and Environmental Justice
Essential Question: How can political institutions govern environmental risks that cross borders, generations, and unequal communities?
Focus: Climate science-policy interface, common but differentiated responsibilities, adaptation, mitigation, energy transition, resource conflict, environmental justice, Indigenous sovereignty, and treaty design.
Source Laboratory: IPCC summaries, climate agreements, emissions data, adaptation plans, and environmental-justice cases

Unit: Unit 7 · Development, Political Economy, and Global Challenges
Title: War, Civil Conflict, and Peacebuilding
Essential Question: Why do conflicts begin, persist, end, and sometimes recur?
Focus: Interstate war, civil war, grievance, opportunity, security dilemmas, commitment problems, identity, external intervention, mediation, ceasefires, peace agreements, justice, and reconstruction.
Source Laboratory: Peace agreements, conflict datasets, mediation records, and post-conflict evaluations

Unit: Unit 7 · Development, Political Economy, and Global Challenges
Title: Security, Terrorism, Nuclear Risk, and Cyber Conflict
Essential Question: How should societies address severe security threats while preserving law, evidence, proportionality, and human rights?
Focus: Traditional and human security, terrorism, radicalization, counterterrorism, deterrence, proliferation, arms control, cyber operations, attribution, resilience, and emergency power.
Source Laboratory: Security Council records, arms-control treaties, threat assessments, court cases, and cyber incident reports

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Technology, AI, Surveillance, and Digital Rights
Essential Question: How should law and democratic governance respond when digital systems redistribute information, power, labor, privacy, and risk?
Focus: Artificial intelligence, automated decisions, algorithmic bias, privacy, surveillance, facial recognition, platform governance, data sovereignty, cyber rights, intellectual property, and accountability.
Source Laboratory: AI governance frameworks, privacy law, algorithmic audits, platform policies, and rights cases

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Public Health and Humanitarian Coordination
Essential Question: What makes collective response legitimate and effective during cross-border health and humanitarian emergencies?
Focus: Public health authority, surveillance, risk communication, World Health Organization, emergency coordination, supply chains, equity, misinformation, humanitarian principles, and after-action review.
Source Laboratory: WHO regulations and reports, national response records, humanitarian standards, and public-health data

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Capstone Evidence and Findings
Essential Question: Can the student transform a documented body of evidence into transparent, appropriately qualified findings?
Focus: Coding, quantitative and qualitative analysis, pattern identification, triangulation, negative cases, uncertainty, tables, figures, findings, and limitations.
Source Laboratory: Student evidence corpus, analysis log, data tables, and methods record

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Thesis Drafting and Peer Review
Essential Question: How can revision improve reasoning, evidence, organization, fairness, and academic integrity?
Focus: Thesis architecture, literature review, methods, findings, analysis, counterargument, implications, citations, peer review, revision memo, and final editing.
Performance: Complete Thesis Draft and Revision Memorandum
Source Laboratory: Complete draft, rubric, citation record, peer feedback, and version history

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Political Engagement and Public Communication
Essential Question: How can a graduate communicate research and engage responsibly without manipulating evidence or compelling political conformity?
Focus: Stakeholder engagement, public audience, neutral civic options, accessibility, testimony, briefings, infographics, public comments, service, reflection, and ethical boundaries.
Performance: Political Engagement Report and Public Presentation
Source Laboratory: Stakeholder records, public meeting materials, civic resources, and student communication products

Unit: Unit 8 · Technology, Health, and Senior Synthesis
Title: Senior Thesis, Oral Defense, and Cumulative Final
Essential Question: Can the student independently defend a rigorous conclusion, acknowledge limits, apply four years of social studies, and satisfy every graduation gate?
Focus: Final thesis, executive summary, public product, oral presentation, questioning, cumulative examination, portfolio audit, evaluator verification, and final credit decision.
Performance: Senior Thesis, Oral Defense, Cumulative Final, and Credit Review
Source Laboratory: Final course portfolio, thesis, examination, defense record, and graduation audit
Capstone Checkpoint: Final Thesis, Defense, and Portfolio Audit
